criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community drinking-water service access via the functionality of 5,921 improved community water points across 15 rural districts in Tanzania covering 15% of the rural population.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper passes because alongside water point technology and age it empirically analyses local community O&M management practices (whether management meetings were held, whether any income was collected, and whether O&M expenditure occurred in the previous year) and discusses community water management models (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include'). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism clarification, however, Criterion 2 is NOT met (c2_legal_admin_factor = 'no'): the study does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff or cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or variation in utility ownership/regulatory structure). The authors explicitly state that 'the governance structure is the same for all regions', the survey merely records generic binary O&M activity indicators (meetings held, any income collected for unspecified purposes, any expenditure made) alongside hardware technology and age, and the 1991 National Water Policy shift is mentioned only as unanalysed macro-governance historical background.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical quantitative study analysing Water Point Mapping (WPM) survey data from 5,921 improved water points (5,852 with construction year) collected in 2005-2006 using Pearson's chi-square tests and linear trend regressions across 5-year construction cohorts.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports water point functionality rates (whether an improved water point yields water regularly and is used on a day-to-day basis vs. non-functional), directly capturing community water service availability and reliability over time.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies unit of analysis and sample (5,921 improved rural water points in 15 districts of Tanzania), exposures (technology category, years since construction, and binary prior-year O&M indicators: meetings held, income collected, expenditure incurred), outcome (water point functionality), and study design (cross-sectional water point mapping survey).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper presents an analysis of the relationships between technology of water point, management related practices and functionality over time through an extensive water point mapping study made in 15 rural districts of Tanzania, which covered 15% of the total rural population of the country.

The aim of the study is to establish the relationships between technology, functionality and durability of rural water points, based on the review of WPM data from 5,921 improved water points. Data were collected between 2005 and 2006 by Wateraid.

One water point (WP) is considered to be functional if it yields water regularly and is being used by people as a water source on a day to day basis. A WP is non-functional if it does not yield water for any reason, whether due to a hardware problem, to the source being dry, or to poor management.

The analysis of the questions dealing with management at the community level did not yield conclusive results. Positive management practices were not exclusive of functional WPs, and, conversely, negative ones were not exclusive of non-functional WPs, as one might expect a priori.
Since the governance structure is the same for all regions, we analysed the relationship with general poverty indicators.

raw_response.exposure: Water point technology category (handpumps, motorised pumping systems, gravity-fed systems, others), years since construction, and generic community O&M activity indicators in the prior year (meetings held, income collected, expenditure made)
raw_response.outcome: Water point functionality status (whether the improved water point yields water regularly and is used on a day-to-day basis)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 5,921 improved rural community water points (5,852 with year of construction) mapped across 15 rural districts in Tanzania covering 15% of the rural population (unit of analysis: water point)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically examines rural water point functionality (service availability/reliability) across 5,921 mapped water points in Tanzania, its analysed exposures are hardware technology type, years since construction, and generic operational O&M activity indicators (whether meetings were held, whether any income was collected for unspecified purposes, and whether O&M expenditure occurred in the prior year). The authors explicitly note that the governance structure is identical across all studied regions, and no rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, tariff/cost-recovery rule, eligibility, tenure, enforcement, or ownership/regulatory mechanism directly governing service access is analysed (national water policy is referenced only as unanalysed historical background). Under the broader plain wording of Criterion 2, the local community O&M management variables would qualify, so plain_criterion2_decision is recorded as 'include'.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional quantitative survey (Water Point Mapping of 5,921 improved water points using Pearson's chi-square tests and cohort linear regression)
